t: Solemnity of the Octave of Christmas
b: Eight days after Christmas the Church names Mary Theotokos, 'God-bearer', the title the Council of Ephesus (431) defended: the child she bore is God. The day is also the World Day of Peace and the feast of the circumcision and naming of Jesus (Luke 2:21).

n: Basil the Great and Gregory Nazianzen
t: Bishops and Doctors of the Church
b: Two friends from student days in Athens who became the great theologians of the Trinity against Arianism. Basil organised monastic life in the East and built a hospital city for the poor; Gregory, 'the Theologian', preached the five orations on the divinity of Christ that shaped the Creed.

n: The Most Holy Name of Jesus
b: 'Thou shalt call his name Jesus, for he shall save his people from their sins' (Matt 1:21). The devotion to the Name spread through Bernardine of Siena, who carried the monogram IHS through the cities of Italy. Also remembered today: Saint Genevieve, the shepherdess who saved Paris from Attila by prayer.

A New York widow with five children who entered the Catholic Church in 1805 at great social cost, founded the Sisters of Charity and the first free Catholic school for girls in America. The first native-born citizen of the United States to be canonised (1975).

A Bohemian who came to America because his own diocese had too many priests, walked the frontier of upstate New York as a missionary, joined the Redemptorists, and as bishop of Philadelphia built the first diocesan school system in the country. He spoke eight languages so that immigrants could confess in their own.

t: Solemnity (kept on the nearest Sunday in many countries)
b: The manifestation of Christ to the nations: the Magi following the star to Bethlehem, and by ancient tradition also his baptism in the Jordan and the wedding at Cana. Older than Christmas in the East, the feast closes the Twelve Days.

A Catalan canon lawyer who compiled the Decretals for Pope Gregory IX, became master general of the Dominicans, and encouraged Thomas Aquinas to write the Summa contra Gentiles for the conversion of the Moors. He lived to be a hundred. Patron of lawyers.

A mysterious monk who appeared on the Danube as the Roman Empire collapsed, organised food for starving towns, negotiated with barbarian kings, and foretold the rise of Odoacer. His disciples carried his body to Naples when they fled.

An African-born abbot who twice refused the see of Canterbury and instead accompanied Theodore of Tarsus to England, where for forty years he ran the school at Canterbury that taught Greek, Latin, astronomy and Scripture to the English Church.

Younger brother of Basil the Great, the most philosophical of the Cappadocian Fathers. His Life of Moses reads the Exodus as the soul's endless ascent into God — 'to find God is to seek him without end.' Called 'father of fathers' by the Second Council of Nicaea.

Founder of a great monastery near Bethlehem with hospitals for the sick, the aged and the mentally ill, and churches where Greeks, Armenians and Bessians each prayed in their own language. He defied the emperor Anastasius over the Council of Chalcedon and lived to 105.

Steward at the court of King David of Scotland, then a Cistercian monk and abbot of Rievaulx in Yorkshire, where he ruled six hundred monks with a gentleness that made him 'the Bernard of the North'. His treatise Spiritual Friendship is the medieval classic on friendship in Christ.

t: Bishop and Doctor of the Church
b: A married pagan philosopher who found God in the opening of John's Gospel, was made bishop of Poitiers, and was exiled to Phrygia for refusing to condemn Athanasius. There he wrote On the Trinity, the first great Latin defence of the divinity of Christ. 'The Athanasius of the West.'

A priest of Nola tortured in the Decian persecution and hidden, legend says, by a spider's web spun over the mouth of his hiding place. He refused a bishopric and gave away his land to the poor; Paulinus of Nola wrote a poem for his feast every year for fourteen years.

Fled the Decian persecution into the Egyptian desert about 250 and lived there ninety years, fed by a raven, according to Jerome's Life of Paul. Anthony the Great found him at the end and buried him in the cloak of Athanasius; two lions, the story says, dug the grave.

Elected after a four-year vacancy under Diocletian, he reorganised the Roman Church into parishes and insisted on penance for those who had apostatised in the persecution. The resulting riots led the emperor Maxentius to banish him; tradition says he was condemned to work as a stable groom.

Hearing 'Go, sell what thou hast, and give to the poor' read in church, a young Egyptian farmer did exactly that and went into the desert, where he fought demons, counselled emperors by letter, and lived to 105. Athanasius's Life of Anthony converted Augustine and set Europe's monasteries in motion.

Daughter of King Béla IV, promised to God before birth if Hungary were delivered from the Mongols. She refused two royal marriages, took the veil on the Danube island that now bears her name, and chose the hardest work of the convent. Also today: the Chair of Peter (traditional calendar).

A Danish king who built churches, protected the poor and levied a tithe for the clergy, and was murdered by rebels at the altar of St Alban's church in Odense. The first Dane to be canonised. Also today: Saints Marius, Martha and their sons, Persian martyrs at Rome.

Fabian, a layman chosen pope when a dove settled on his head, died in the Decian persecution of 250. Sebastian, a Roman officer of the Praetorian guard, was shot with arrows for his faith, nursed back to health by Irene, and clubbed to death when he confronted Diocletian — the arrows made him the most painted of martyrs.

A Roman girl of about twelve who refused marriage and sacrifice under Diocletian and was killed by the sword. Her name sounds like agnus, lamb: on her feast two lambs are blessed in Rome whose wool becomes the pallia of archbishops. Ambrose, Jerome and Augustine all preached about her.

Deacon of Saragossa, tortured on the rack and the gridiron at Valencia under Diocletian; his composure so shook his judge Dacian that the story of it spread through the whole Church. Augustine said his passion was read 'in every land under the sun'. Patron of vintners.

A Franciscan sister of Syracuse, New York, who answered the king of Hawaii's plea for nurses when fifty other congregations had refused, and spent thirty-five years among the lepers of Molokai, promising her sisters they would never catch the disease. None did.

t: Bishop and Doctor of the Church
b: Bishop of Geneva who could not enter his own Calvinist city, so he slid leaflets under doors — the first religious tracts — and won back the Chablais by gentleness. His Introduction to the Devout Life taught laypeople that holiness is for everyone. Patron of writers and journalists.

On the road to Damascus, breathing threats, Saul of Tarsus was knocked to the ground by a light and a voice: 'Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me?' Three days blind, then baptised by Ananias, he became the apostle to the Gentiles. The Week of Prayer for Christian Unity ends today.

Paul's two closest lieutenants and the recipients of three of his letters. Timothy, half Greek and half Jew, was left in charge of Ephesus; Titus, a Greek, of Crete. Tradition says Timothy was beaten to death for opposing a festival of Diana, and Titus died old in Gortyna.

A Franciscan tertiary of Brescia who gathered unmarried women to teach girls in their own homes — the Ursulines, the first teaching order of women, founded thirty years before Trent and without cloister, a scandal in her century.

t: Priest and Doctor of the Church
b: The 'dumb ox' of Aquino whose Summa Theologiae is the cathedral of medieval thought. His family imprisoned him to stop him joining the Dominicans; he escaped, studied under Albert the Great, and wrote until a vision at Mass made him say 'all I have written seems like straw'. He died on the way to the Council of Lyon.

A British monk whose furious sermon On the Ruin of Britain is almost the only written witness to the century when the Saxons conquered the island — the age Arthurian legend remembers. He ended his days as a hermit on an island off Brittany.

A Roman deacon's daughter martyred under Alexander Severus; her relics were found beneath the Forum in 1634 and Bernini's Santi Luca e Martina was built over them. Also today: Hyacintha Mariscotti, the vain nun who became an ascetic and founder of confraternities for the poor.

A Piedmontese peasant's son who learned juggling to draw boys to catechism, and in industrial Turin gathered the street children into an oratory where they were fed, taught a trade and loved. 'Don Bosco' founded the Salesians, now the second-largest religious order in the world.

A slave's daughter who, legend says, gave away her father's sword to a beggar, founded the double monastery of Kildare where a perpetual fire burned for a thousand years, and became with Patrick and Columba a patron of Ireland. The rush cross woven on her eve still hangs in Irish homes.

wp: Presentation of Jesus at the Temple
b: Forty days after his birth Jesus is carried into the Temple, and old Simeon takes him in his arms: 'a light to the revelation of the Gentiles.' Candles are blessed and carried in procession — Candlemas — and the Christmas cycle finally closes.

A physician-bishop of Sebaste in Armenia, said to have saved a boy choking on a fishbone; hence the blessing of throats with crossed candles on his day. Martyred under Licinius by being torn with iron wool-combs. Also today: Ansgar, apostle of Scandinavia.

A wild Florentine youth converted by his mother's reproach, he became a Carmelite, bishop of Fiesole, and the peacemaker of Tuscany's warring factions. Also today: John de Brito, Portuguese Jesuit martyred in India in 1693 for refusing to leave his converts.

A Sicilian noblewoman of Catania who refused the consul Quintianus and was tortured, her breasts cut off, under Decius. Her veil is carried against eruptions of Etna. Named in the Roman Canon of the Mass with Agnes, Cecilia, Lucy and Anastasia.

Twenty-six Christians — Jesuits, Franciscans and laymen, three of them boys — crucified on a hill above Nagasaki after being marched six hundred miles through winter. Paul Miki, a Japanese Jesuit, preached forgiveness from his cross. Two centuries later missionaries found the hidden Christians still keeping the faith.

A young Ravenna nobleman who watched his father kill a man in a duel and fled to a monastery in horror; he spent his life founding hermitages that joined the solitude of the desert to the common life. 'Sit in your cell as in paradise.' (Kept on June 19 in the new calendar.)

Kidnapped in Darfur at seven, sold five times, scarred by her owners, she was brought to Italy, learned of Christ from the Canossian sisters and refused to go back to Sudan — an Italian court ruled she was free. She spent fifty years as a humble sister in Schio. Patroness of Sudan and of victims of trafficking. Also today: Jerome Emiliani.

An aged deaconess of Alexandria seized by a mob that broke her teeth, then threatened her with fire unless she blasphemed; she asked a moment as if to consider, and leapt into the flames. Invoked against toothache. Bishop Dionysius, who knew her, tells the story.

Twin sister of Benedict, and a nun near Monte Cassino. At their last yearly meeting she begged him to stay the night talking of heaven; when he refused, she prayed, and a storm broke so violent he could not leave. Three days later he saw her soul rise as a dove. Gregory the Great tells it: 'she who loved more, could do more.'

t: Optional memorial · World Day of the Sick
b: On 11 February 1858 a fourteen-year-old peasant girl, Bernadette Soubirous, saw a lady in a grotto by the Gave who later said, 'I am the Immaculate Conception' — words the child did not understand. Millions have since drunk from the spring; the Church has recognised seventy cures as miraculous.

n: The Seven Founders of the Servite Order
b: Seven Florentine cloth merchants who left their businesses in 1233 to live in penance on Monte Senario, and founded the Servants of Mary, devoted to her sorrows. The last of them, Alexis Falconieri, lived to 110. (Kept on February 17 in the new calendar.)

A Dominican nun of Prato who for twelve years relived the Passion every week from Thursday noon to Friday afternoon, corresponded with three future popes, and reformed her convent with practical good sense. Philip Neri, who never left Rome, is said to have conversed with her in a vision.

t: Bishop; monk — apostles of the Slavs, patrons of Europe
b: Two brothers from Thessalonica who translated the Scriptures and the liturgy into Slavonic, inventing an alphabet to do it, and defended a Slavic liturgy before the pope against German bishops who allowed only Hebrew, Greek and Latin. Also today: Valentine, the martyr-priest of Rome.

Spiritual director of Margaret Mary Alacoque at Paray-le-Monial, who believed her visions of the Sacred Heart when no one else did; later chaplain to the Duchess of York in London, imprisoned in the Popish Plot, and sent home to die at forty-one.

The slave of Philemon who fled to Paul in prison and was sent back with the shortest letter in the New Testament — 'receive him as myself.' Tradition makes him bishop of Ephesus after Timothy and a martyr at Rome. Also today: Juliana of Nicomedia, virgin martyr.

n: Alexis Falconieri and the Seven Holy Founders
b: See February 12 in the traditional calendar: seven merchants of Florence who became the Servants of Mary. Alexis alone refused the priesthood and begged for the community's bread. Also today: Finan of Lindisfarne, who baptised the kings of Mercia and the East Saxons.

The girl of Lourdes, who after the apparitions entered the Sisters of Charity at Nevers and was set to work in the infirmary: 'I was a broom Our Lady used; she has put me back in my corner.' She died at thirty-five of tuberculosis of the bone; her body lies incorrupt at Nevers.

A nobleman whose hunting fire got out of control and burned the countryside; when an innocent man was condemned for it, Conrad confessed, paid with his whole fortune, and with his wife's agreement became a Franciscan hermit in Sicily, famous for his gentleness with birds.

Brother and sister, nine and seven, who with their cousin Lúcia saw the Lady at Fatima in 1917. Both died in the influenza epidemic within three years, as she had told them they would; Jacinta offered her lonely hospital death for sinners. The youngest non-martyrs ever canonised.

t: Bishop and Doctor of the Church
b: An orphan who tended pigs, then a hermit of Fonte Avellana and, against his will, cardinal-bishop of Ostia, the fiercest reformer of a corrupt eleventh-century clergy. Dante places him in the sphere of Saturn among the contemplatives.

Not a relic but an office: the teaching authority of Peter and his successors, celebrated in Rome since the fourth century. 'Thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church' (Matt 16:18). Bernini's bronze throne in St Peter's encloses an ancient wooden chair.

A disciple of the apostle John, burned in the stadium of Smyrna at eighty-six: 'Eighty-six years have I served him, and he has done me no wrong; how can I blaspheme my King who saved me?' The account of his death is the oldest martyrdom narrative after Stephen's.

Chosen by lot to replace Judas, 'that he might take part in this ministry and apostleship' (Acts 1:25). Tradition sends him to Ethiopia or Cappadocia and gives him a martyr's death. (Kept on May 14 in the new calendar.)

An English nun, niece of Boniface, who followed him to Germany and ruled the double monastery of Heidenheim. Oil that flows from the rock of her tomb at Eichstätt has been collected for a thousand years. The eve of her May feast gave Walpurgisnacht its name.

A monk of the Egyptian desert made bishop of Gaza, then the most stubbornly pagan city in Palestine. He went to Constantinople and obtained from the empress an order to close the temples; the great temple of Marnas was burned and a church built on its ashes.

t: Monk and Doctor of the Church
b: An Armenian monk whose Book of Lamentations — ninety-five prayers 'speaking with God from the depths of the heart' — is kept under the pillow of the sick in Armenia to this day. Pope Francis named him Doctor of the Church in 2015. Also today: Gabriel Possenti, the young Passionist.

Two brothers who founded the first monasteries in the Jura mountains, Condat and Lauconne, drawing so many that a third had to be built for their sister. Romanus was gentle, Lupicinus severe; between them they filled the forests of Burgundy with monks.

A Dane by blood, bishop of Worcester and archbishop of York, who with Dunstan and Ethelwold revived English monasticism after the Viking wars. He died on his knees, having washed the feet of twelve poor men, as he did every day in Lent.

Founder of the monastery of Menevia (St Davids), where the monks pulled the plough themselves and drank only water — 'David the Waterman'. At the synod of Brefi, legend says, the ground rose under him so that all could hear. His last words: 'Do the little things.'

Brother of Cedd, pupil of Aidan, bishop of the Mercians at Lichfield, who walked everywhere until Archbishop Theodore lifted him bodily onto a horse. Bede loved him: when the wind rose, Chad would stop and pray, 'because the Lord moves the air to remind us of the judgment.'

Heiress of a Philadelphia banking fortune who asked Leo XIII to send missionaries to the Indians, and was told, 'Why not become one yourself?' She founded the Sisters of the Blessed Sacrament and spent twenty million dollars on schools for Black and Native Americans, including Xavier University.

Second son of the king of Poland, who refused the Hungarian crown his father tried to win for him by war, wore a hair shirt under his royal robes, and died of tuberculosis at twenty-five. Patron of Poland and Lithuania; the hymn Omni die dic Mariae was found in his coffin.

A Neapolitan noble who joined the Alcantarine Franciscans at sixteen, walked barefoot, slept three hours a night, and was so besieged by the sick of Naples that he had to be protected by the friars. Also today: Piran, the Cornish abbot who floated from Ireland on a millstone.

t: Virgin, reformer of the Poor Clares
b: A carpenter's daughter who lived walled up as an anchoress, then, commanded in a vision by Francis, left her cell to restore the strict rule of Clare; she founded seventeen convents and reconciled the rival popes' followers. She foretold her own death at the hour of Compline.

A young Carthaginian mother of good family and her pregnant slave, thrown to the beasts in the arena on the birthday of the emperor's son. Perpetua's prison diary — the earliest Christian writing by a woman — survives; she guided the gladiator's sword to her own throat. Both are named in the Roman Canon.

A Portuguese soldier, shepherd and bookseller who at forty heard John of Ávila preach and went so mad with remorse that he was locked in an asylum; the cruelty he saw there made him found a hospital in Granada where the sick were treated with mercy. Patron of hospitals and nurses.

A Roman noblewoman who, married at thirteen against her wish, made her palace a refuge for the plague-stricken and the starving during the schism and the wars of Ladislaus, and founded the Oblates of Tor de' Specchi. She saw her guardian angel constantly. Patroness of motorists.

Forty soldiers of the Twelfth Legion left naked on a frozen lake in Armenia under Licinius, with a warm bath on the shore for any who would renounce Christ. One gave in; a guard, seeing forty crowns descending, stripped and took his place. Basil and Gregory of Nyssa preached on them.

A priest of Muslim Córdoba who wrote the Memorial of the Saints to encourage the Christians who publicly confessed Christ and were executed for it, and was himself beheaded for hiding a young convert from Islam, Leocritia.

Prefect of Rome turned monk, then pope in a city of plague and Lombard siege; he fed Rome from the Church's estates, sent Augustine to convert the English, wrote the Pastoral Rule and the Dialogues, and gave his name to the chant. (Kept on September 3 in the new calendar.)

A relative of the emperor Theodosius who at seven entered a convent in Egypt with her widowed mother and, when the emperor summoned her to marry, asked him instead to give her fortune to the poor and free her slaves. She carried stones from place to place to conquer temptation.

Wife of Henry the Fowler and mother of the emperor Otto the Great, who founded monasteries at Quedlinburg and Nordhausen and gave so freely to the poor that her sons accused her of wasting the treasury. She forgave them and outlived the accusation.

A widow of the French court who under Vincent de Paul founded the Daughters of Charity — sisters whose cloister was 'the streets of the city', their chapel the parish church — the first women religious to nurse in the world without enclosure. Patroness of social workers.

A hermit of Edessa who left his cell to convert a pagan village by patience, and years later, disguised as a soldier, walked into a brothel to rescue his niece Mary, who had fled there in despair; he brought her home and she became a saint. Ephrem the Syrian told the story.

A British boy kidnapped by Irish raiders at sixteen, six years a slave herding sheep, who escaped, became a bishop, and returned to the land of his captivity to convert it. His Confession and his Letter to Coroticus are the oldest documents written in Ireland. He used the shamrock, tradition says, to explain the Trinity.

t: Bishop and Doctor of the Church
b: Bishop of Jerusalem exiled three times by the Arians. His Catechetical Lectures, given in the church of the Holy Sepulchre to those about to be baptised, are the fullest picture we have of how the fourth-century Church explained the Creed and the sacraments to newcomers.

n: Joseph, Spouse of the Blessed Virgin Mary
b: The carpenter of Nazareth, 'a just man', who obeyed four dreams, took the pregnant Mary into his home, carried the child to Egypt and back, and taught him a trade. He never speaks in the Gospels. Patron of the universal Church, of workers and of a happy death.

A shepherd boy who saw Aidan's soul carried to heaven and became a monk at Melrose, prior of Lindisfarne, and a hermit on the Inner Farne with the seals and the eider ducks that still bear his name. His body was carried by the monks for a hundred years from the Vikings until it rested at Durham.

The father of Western monks, who left Rome's schools for a cave at Subiaco, founded Monte Cassino, and wrote the Rule — 'a little rule for beginners' — that ordered Europe's prayer and work for fifteen centuries. Today is the day of his death; July 11 is his feast in the new calendar.

'Little John', a carpenter who built priest-holes in the manor houses of Elizabethan England so cunning that some were found only centuries later. Captured after the Gunpowder Plot, he was tortured to death in the Tower without betraying a single hiding place.

A Spanish law professor made archbishop of Lima while still a layman, who learned Quechua, travelled his diocese of eighteen thousand miles on foot three times, confirmed Rose of Lima and Martin de Porres, and fought the conquistadors for the rights of the Indians.

Daughter of Bridget of Sweden, who followed her mother to Rome, lived with her twenty-five years, and carried her body home to Vadstena, where she became abbess of the Bridgettines. Also today: Oscar Romero, archbishop of San Salvador, shot at the altar in 1980.

Nine months before Christmas: Gabriel comes to a girl in Nazareth, and at her 'Be it done to me according to thy word' the Word becomes flesh. For centuries Lady Day was the first day of the year in England. The Angelus, prayed three times daily, is this scene.

A Frisian pupil of Alcuin who rebuilt the missions the pagan Saxons had burned, refused to hurry his morning prayers when Charlemagne summoned him, and became the first bishop of Münster. Also today: Margaret Clitherow, pressed to death at York in 1586 for hiding priests.

A carpenter who walled himself into a cell on a cliff near Lycopolis for fifty years, speaking to visitors through a window on Saturdays and Sundays; the emperor Theodosius twice sent to ask him the outcome of his wars, and both times he answered rightly. Augustine and Jerome mention him.

A monk of St Gall who was poet, sculptor, painter, architect, metalworker, musician and teacher — 'a man of strength and eloquence, skilled in every art', says the chronicler. Some of the earliest tropes of the Mass are his. Ekkehard says he could have been famous and chose to be a monk.

Two Persian monks who visited Christians condemned by King Shapur II and were arrested for it; the acts of their torture are among the most detailed of the Persian persecution. Also today: Gwynllyw and Gwladys, Welsh king and queen who ended as hermits.

Abbot of St Catherine's on Mount Sinai, named for his Ladder of Divine Ascent — thirty steps from renunciation to love, read aloud in Orthodox monasteries every Lent to this day. He had lived forty years as a hermit before being made abbot.

A Persian deacon imprisoned for preaching, released at the request of the Roman ambassador on condition of silence, who kept preaching and was executed by having reeds driven under his nails. Also today: Guy of Pomposa, the abbot Dante's teacher Peter Damian admired.
